catalog_quote: Of the Dogon languages I have worked on, DS and Dogul Dom come closest to satisfying a pitch-accent (i.e. tonal accent) model. At the lexical level, each noncomposite stem (verb, noun, etc.) has exactly one H-toned syllable or mora. This can be handled by a model with an obligatory, one-per-word H-tone accent. At word-level too, after all phonological rules have operated, there is almost always exactly one H-toned syllable or mora, except when all tones have dropped due to tonosyntactic control or (in the case of clause-final verbs) downdrift. The reason this model will work fairly well for DS is that it has no words with adjacent-syllable H-tones. ... new_statements.rule_in_words: Donno So is described as a tone language with one lexically H-toned syllable or mora per stem (no all-L stems, no adjacent H syllables, no /HLH/), which Heath says approximates a one-accent-per-word pitch accent system. The position of the H is lexical: verbs are /HL/ (accent on the initial syllable) or /LH/ (accent final), fixed for obstruent-initial verbs and lexical for others; nouns, adjectives and numerals are /HL/, /LHL/ or /LH/ (H on first, medial or last syllable; in /HL/ nonmonosyllabics the H is on the initial syllable). Lexical melodies are regularly overridden by grammatical {L} tone overlays. Heath adds a caveat (p. 32) that H may fall on either mora of a bimoraic syllable (kɛ̂y vs kɛ̌y, bôy vs bǒy), so DS cannot be equated with syllable-based pitch accent languages. No mention of stress or intensity prominence for DS anywhere in the grammar.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed (no stress discussed); at word level there is generally only one H-tone, with a few exceptions in nominal compounds and periphrastic verb inflections that may carry two H-tones (p. 29).
new_statements.exceptions: Lexically L-toned grammatical particles and stative quasi-verbs (sɛ̀ 'have', wɔ̀ 'be', nàmà 'want'); a few all-L expressive adverbials (§8.4.7); compounds and complex hortatives/periphrastic inflections with two H-tones; all tones drop under tonosyntactic {L} overlay or clause-final downdrift (pp. 29, 32).
new_statements.domain_note: Stem- and word-level lexical tone; word-level generalisation applies after phonological rules, with phrase-level tonosyntactic overlays (tone-dropping) removing the H entirely. Heath's data are from the Wendegele dialect (p. 157 contrasts his imperfective -dɛ̀ 'in the Wendegele dialect' with K&P's -zɛ). Kervran & Prost 1969 apparently posited an 'accent d'intensité' separate from tone (Heath p. 157), which Heath reinterprets as /LH/ tone.
new_statements.identity_note: Heath's grammar covers Donno So = Kamma So (glottocode donn1239, ISO dds); his own data are from the Wendegele dialect (he contrasts his imperfective -dɛ̀ 'in the Wendegele dialect' with Kervran & Prost's -zɛ, p. 157). Kervran & Prost 1969/1986 and Kervran's dictionaries describe the Bandiagara-region variety of the same language. Glottolog cites the 2014 draft (439 pp.); the 2016 Language Description Heritage version (384 pp.) is the current one and was quoted.
